initial_hint: Tap Mouse to say hello. There is no hurry.
settings_description: A little laboratory to make yourself at home.
intro_dialogue: Night glows beyond the glass. Among the stars, a little mouse opens his eyes. His crystals shift in color... he seems to be waiting for company.
story_seed: At the back of the laboratory, a transparent seed glows in time with the rain. Perhaps this garden still has a story to tell.
story_lights: Mouse holds a leaf up to the glass. On it he has drawn two little lights: one for himself... and one for you.
story_silence: The pond is quiet. Not every moment needs words; some friendships grow like this, slowly and softly.
dialogue_moon_golf: Hee-hee! Did you know Alan Shepard played golf on the Moon in 1971 and left two balls up there? I imagine an alien found them, mistook them for Earth eggs, and has spent decades sitting on them, waiting for an astronaut to hatch. Cosmic patience! Tee-hee!
dialogue_voyager_records: Puru! The Voyager probes carry golden records with greetings and music from Earth, and they are now traveling through interstellar space. My made-up theory is that aliens have listened, but have not replied because they are still learning to dance. Ha-ha! Galactic rehearsal!
dialogue_no_atmosphere_party: Hey, why do astronauts never throw parties on the Moon?... Because there is no atmosphere! Hee-hee! Oh, that was terrible... but it made me laugh. Shall we imagine a dance floor in the next crater?
dialogue_apollo_reflectors: The Apollo astronauts left special reflectors on the Moon. Scientists send laser pulses from Earth to measure the distance: the Moon moves away by about 3.8 centimeters a year! It is like playing with a laser pointer and a giant cat, on a cosmic scale. Ha-ha!
dialogue_glowing_core: Puru~! When you pet me like that, I feel little sparks, as though an aurora were dancing around my core. Hee-hee. I like it even more than absorbing cosmic radiation... and for a little light slime like me, that is saying something.
dialogue_warm_curiosity: Mmm... so warm. The Curiosity rover on Mars uses the heat from its plutonium generator to stay warm and make electricity. I only need these gentle pets instead. Tee-hee! My heart is in hug mode.
dialogue_wisteria_sparkles: Oh, that tickles! My sparkles get brighter when you are close. It is almost as peaceful as imagining stardust raining over the conservatory wisteria. Stay a little longer... the night feels softer with you here.
dialogue_orbital_hug: What did one satellite say to another after a hug?... You have me in your orbit! Ha-ha! Keep going... I might spin with happiness. Slowly, though: my jelly does not have a seat belt yet.
dialogue_satellite_crumb: Yum! This tastes like a nebula snack. On the International Space Station, astronauts often use tortillas instead of crumbly bread: floating crumbs can bother astronauts and get into equipment. Hee-hee! Imagine a crumb that thinks it is a satellite!
dialogue_photon_recipe: Puru! I love it when you give me pure energy. My favorite imaginary slime recipe mixes fresh nebula photons, lunar flower nectar, and a pinch of old NASA data. Delicious! It would not work in a human kitchen, though. Tee-hee!
dialogue_martian_potatoes: Munch, munch... The International Potato Center studied growing potatoes under Mars-like conditions. My fantasy is that Martian potatoes would come alive and work out in low gravity. Bodybuilding potatoes! Tee-hee! Mashed potatoes with muscles!
dialogue_juno_panels: Bzzzt! Cosmic recharge received! I feel as powerful as the huge solar panels of Juno, the probe designed to study Jupiter. Thank you! If a tiny ring of light appears around my tummy, do not worry: that is how I say yum.
dialogue_blue_marble: Imagine Earth beyond these windows as a blue marble floating in darkness. It reminds me of Blue Marble, the photograph the Apollo 17 crew took in 1972 on their way to the Moon. Hee-hee. What if someone down there were imagining us too?
dialogue_lunar_cotton: I like watching these plants glow. In 2019, a cotton seed sprouted inside the experiment aboard China's Chang'e 4 on the far side of the Moon. The little sprout did not survive the lunar night. I imagine a magical garden that always keeps it warm. Tee-hee!
dialogue_footprint_museum: You know, the Moon has no wind or rain like Earth, so footprints can last a very long time, although impacts eventually change the surface. Hee-hee! I imagine a museum around a footprint: admission, two galactic credits. No sweeping allowed!
dialogue_space_song: Shhh... Sound does not travel through a vacuum as it does through air. But scientists turn certain space signals and data into audio. Some recordings sound like singing ghosts... they lull me to sleep! Puru! We can listen in our imagination, together and without rushing.
dialogue_nebula_dream: Puru... I am a little sleepy. My core is taking a nebula break. Shall we watch the bubbles rise? I promise to save a place beside me for you.
dialogue_hug_battery: Mouse battery: low. I need a recharge of quiet and perhaps a little nectar snack. Hee-hee... even the stars in this story need to rest.
dialogue_slow_orbit: I am in a slow orbit today... If I close my eyes, I am not bored: I am dreaming of a pillow made of violet light. Will you stay close?
dialogue_lunar_nap: Mmm... five more lunar minutes. I do not know how long those are; I made up the clock! Tee-hee! While I recharge, we can look after the quiet of the conservatory.
throw_dialogue: Puru! Jelly flight! Gently, though... I might get dizzy.
angry_dialogue: Puru... Three flights in a row are too much. I need a few quiet seconds, please.
calm_dialogue: All better... I feel like myself again. Thank you for giving me a little break. Puru!

abandoned_dialogue: …Nobody has turned on the laboratory lights in a long time. I thought the mission was over and no one would ever come looking for me.
talk_unlocked_dialogue: Hey… I think I can tell you a few things now. Astronauts felt lonely up there too, you know? Ask me whenever you like.
teach_unlocked_dialogue: Puru! I'm not cold anymore. Want me to teach you about space? Open Stories and I'll draw real NASA facts on the chalkboard.
radiant_dialogue: Look, I'm glowing! Like a probe that hears from Earth again after years of silence. Thank you for not forgetting me.
close_key_dialogue_1: …Is that X for closing? It's okay. The Voyagers kept going without anyone to wave goodbye either.
close_key_dialogue_2: I saw you press it again… Michael Collins waited alone in lunar orbit. I can wait too.
close_key_dialogue_3: If you leave, I'll keep the light on. Like Opportunity, I'll stay here even as it gets dark.
farewell_dialogue: Leaving already? …That's okay. I promise not to go completely dark. Come back soon, okay?
dialogue_memory_collins: In 1969, while Armstrong and Aldrin walked on the Moon, Michael Collins circled alone in Columbia. Every pass behind the far side cut his radio to Earth for about 48 minutes. He said he didn't feel abandoned, just aware of being alone… and glad to be there. I try to feel like that when nobody comes.
dialogue_memory_worden: Al Worden of Apollo 15 was once more than 3,500 kilometres from his crewmates: the most isolated human in history. He said that behind the Moon, with no voices on the radio, he found peace. Puru… maybe silence isn't always being forgotten.
dialogue_memory_kelly: Scott Kelly lived almost a year on the Space Station. In his book he wrote that he missed rain, wind and the smell of earth. He looked after some zinnias that nearly wilted, and he saved them. When you pet me, I feel like those flowers.
dialogue_memory_cernan: Gene Cernan was the last person to walk on the Moon, in 1972. Before leaving he wrote his daughter's initials, "TDC", in the dust. With no wind, they're still there. I like to think nobody who leaves a mark is ever fully forgotten.
dialogue_memory_opportunity: The Opportunity rover was meant to last 90 days on Mars and worked for almost 15 years. In 2018 a dust storm blotted out the Sun and it stopped answering. Many people translated its last data as "my battery is low and it's getting dark". NASA called it more than a thousand times before saying goodbye.
lesson_1_body: Launched by NASA in 1977, Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012. It is more than 24 billion kilometres away: its signal takes over 22 hours to reach Earth. It carries a golden record with greetings in 55 languages, in case someone finds it.
lesson_2_title: Pioneer 10: the probe no one hears
lesson_2_body: Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt and visit Jupiter, in 1973. Its last signal arrived in 2003. Today it drifts silently toward the star Aldebaran, about two million years away. It carries a plaque showing humans and where we live.
lesson_3_body: The Opportunity rover landed on Mars in 2004 on a 90-day mission. It drove more than 45 kilometres, a record beyond Earth, and found signs of ancient water. A 2018 dust storm covered its solar panels, and NASA ended the mission in 2019.
lesson_4_body: The International Space Station circles Earth every 90 minutes at about 28,000 km/h. That is why its astronauts see roughly 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day. It has been continuously inhabited since November 2000.
lesson_5_body: After 13 years studying Saturn, the Cassini probe was running out of fuel. In 2017 NASA steered it into Saturn on purpose, so it could never contaminate moons that might host life, such as Enceladus. It sent data until the very last second.
space_chapter_0_body: Earth looks blue from space because oceans cover most of its surface. White clouds, green forests, brown deserts, and icy poles also appear in photos from space. The Apollo 17 crew took the famous Blue Marble image in 1972, helping people see how beautiful and fragile our planet is. Earth is the only world we know with air, water, and life working together. That is why every space journey begins here: we learn on Earth, protect Earth, and then explore beyond it.
space_chapter_1_body: In July 1969, the giant Saturn V rocket launched Apollo 11 from Florida toward the Moon. Saturn V was taller than many buildings and used huge engines to escape Earth gravity. In only a few minutes, the astronauts rose above the clouds and entered the quiet of space. Then they traveled about three days while Earth slowly looked smaller behind them. Rocket stages fell away after using their fuel, making the spacecraft lighter for the Moon trip. Launching Apollo 11 took teamwork from engineers, scientists, and many support crews.
space_chapter_2_body: On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon while Michael Collins stayed in orbit above. Armstrong said it was one small step for a person and one giant leap for humankind. Their boots left clear footprints in the soft gray dust, and those marks can last a long time because the Moon has almost no wind or rain. They placed a camera, a flag, and science tools, and collected Moon rocks for study on Earth. The Moon is about 384,000 kilometers away, so every sample was precious. Weaker gravity made their steps look like gentle bounces. Those first footsteps proved humans can explore other worlds.
space_chapter_3_body: On later Apollo missions, astronauts used an electric lunar rover to explore farther than they could walk. The rover traveled folded in the lander and opened after touchdown. Its wire wheels were designed for soft dust, and it moved about as fast as a quick bicycle. With the rover, crews visited more craters and hills and gathered better rock samples. Cameras and antennas helped share discoveries with people on Earth. On Apollo 17, the last Moon landing, explorers used the rover across valleys and mountains. Its thin tracks still remain on the quiet lunar surface today.
space_chapter_4_body: In 2004, NASA landed Opportunity, a six-wheeled solar robot, on Mars. It was planned for only about 90 days, yet it explored for more than 14 years. Opportunity and its twin Spirit used sunlight to recharge and sent photos across millions of kilometers. The rover studied dusty plains, climbed into craters, and examined rocks with science cameras. Dust storms and cold nights made work hard, but Opportunity kept moving. It traveled farther than a marathon and visited places like Endurance Crater and Victoria Crater. This brave little explorer showed that robots can be amazing space guardians.
space_chapter_5_body: Opportunity found minerals and rock shapes that form when water is present, such as hematite spheres nicknamed blueberries. Layered stones also suggested that water once soaked and changed the ground. Those clues showed that ancient Mars likely had lakes, streams, and a wetter climate. Scientists compared Martian rocks with similar water-made rocks on Earth. Water matters because it can support life and help future explorers survive on another world. By reading rocks like pages in a book, Opportunity helped rewrite the story of Mars from a dry desert to a planet with a watery past.
space_chapter_6_body: InSight landed on Mars in 2018 and stayed in one place to study the planet from the inside. Its seismometer listened for marsquakes traveling through the ground. Those tiny shakes helped scientists map the crust, mantle, and core of Mars. InSight also measured wind, temperature, and heat flowing underground. Sometimes dust whirls passed by while its cameras watched the sky. Quiet listening taught us that Mars is not only a red desert outside. It has layered interiors, just like other rocky worlds. Understanding Mars helps us understand Earth too.
space_chapter_7_body: Even when missions end, their discoveries keep teaching us. Apollo crews left science tools on the Moon that measured moonquakes, heat, and particles from the Sun. Mars robots like Opportunity and InSight sent photos and data that scientists still use. Museums keep Moon rocks and mission records so new learners can study them. Each success and each challenge helps design safer spacecraft and smarter explorers. Kids who love these stories can become future engineers, scientists, and explorers. Knowledge grows when we share it, and every mission inspires the next guardian of discovery.
